summary: Extends the base ALTO protocol's cost information service so applications can decide not only where to connect but also when. This helps bulk data transfers schedule their traffic. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If a big download could be done at any time, it helps to know when the roads are quietest. This extension lets a program ask the network which times are cheapest, not just which places.

what does repeated mean in alto calendar
subtitle: An ALTO extension that lets a server publish network costs as a time table, so applications can choose when to connect as well as where.

tldr.problem: The base ALTO protocol gives cost guidance for the current time only, so an application that can defer traffic, such as a backup, has to guess what the network will look like later.
tldr.mechanism: An ALTO Cost Calendar is a JSON array of cost values, one per time interval. The Information Resources Directory announces the interval size and count, and the response metadata gives the start time and an optional repeat count.
tldr.outcome: Clients can pick off-peak times from one response and reuse repeated calendars. The extension is backwards compatible with RFC 7285 clients, but it adds risks such as handing attackers a schedule of busy periods.

today: RFC 8896 is a Proposed Standard from November 2020, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the base ALTO protocol in RFC 7285.

sections.title: Why Costs Need a Calendar
sections.content:
The base Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) protocol, RFC 7285, gives overlay applications guidance for choosing hosts, based on things like topological distance. ALTO deliberately does not disseminate network metrics that change frequently. Costs still fluctuate with traffic load, daily patterns of demand and planned events such as network maintenance, holidays or highly publicized events.

An application that wants to use costs at some future time has to estimate the network state then, which the RFC calls at best fragile and brittle. That is a poor fit for applications that can schedule their traffic, for example by deferring backups or other background traffic to off-peak hours.

This document extends RFC 7285 so a server can give network costs for a span of time. A sequence of costs across a time span for a pair of network locations is named an ALTO Cost Calendar. The Filtered Cost Map Service and the Endpoint Cost Service are extended to provide them. The RFC also says gathering several values into one response is expected to save network and storage resources.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking the network 'how busy are you right now?' every few minutes, you ask once for the whole day's busy and quiet times.

sections.title: How a Cost Calendar Works
sections.content:
A Calendar carries two things: an array of values for a metric, one per time interval, and attributes that describe the time scope so the client can interpret the array. The value array can sometimes be a cyclic pattern that repeats.

The attributes are:

  • time-interval-size: the length of each interval, in seconds.
  • number-of-intervals: how many values the Calendar holds.
  • calendar-start-time: when the first value applies.
  • repeated (optional): how many iterations of the Calendar have the same values.

Multiplying the interval size by the number of intervals gives the Calendar's duration. For example, an interval size of 5 minutes with 12 intervals gives 1 hour. The IRD announces attributes without dates, while attributes with time-dependent values appear in the meta section of server responses.

The design avoids a new mode and new media types. It relies on the base rule that implementations MUST ignore unknown fields. A cost entry that was queried as a Calendar is an array instead of a single number, and the array size MUST equal the announced number-of-intervals. If it does not, the client SHOULD ignore the array.

Calendars are not limited to numbers. They can also hold other cost values, such as booleans or strings like medium or open, and ordinal-mode values that vary with time.
sections.eli5: A Calendar is like a bus timetable: it says when the first bus leaves, how long between buses, and how many are listed. Some days' timetables are the same, so it can say 'use this one for 4 days'.

sections.title: Announcing Calendars in the IRD
sections.content:
A server announces Calendars in the Information Resources Directory (IRD) using a calendar-attributes member of a resource's capabilities. It is an array of CalendarAttributes objects, each listing cost-type-names plus a time-interval-size and number-of-intervals that apply to them. Cost types that share the same values are grouped in one object.

A cost type name MUST NOT appear more than once. If it does, the client ignores occurrences after the first, or it MAY ignore all of them and query that cost type the base way. The server SHOULD announce the smallest interval size it can provide, and a client that needs longer intervals can aggregate values.

Because attributes belong to an information resource rather than to a cost type, one server can offer the same cost type at different granularities. The RFC's example gives a routingcost Calendar of 6 intervals of 4 hours in a voluminous cost map, and 24 intervals of 1 hour in an endpoint cost map. The RFC also describes delegating Calendar resources to another ALTO server in a subdomain through an IRD with media type application/alto-directory+json.
sections.eli5: Before you ask for a timetable, the server posts a menu saying which timetables exist and how detailed each one is.

sections.title: Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Calendars are available through two services: the Filtered Cost Map and the Endpoint Cost Service. Full cost maps are excluded, because a legacy client fetching one with an HTTP GET would ignore the Calendar attributes in meta and could not interpret the array. Calendared resources MUST be requested with a POST.

A Calendar-aware client adds a calendared member to its request: an array of booleans, one per requested cost type, which MUST have exactly that many entries or the server returns an error. If it is absent, all values are assumed false, and a true value for a cost type without Calendar attributes is ignored, so the server returns a single value. Constraints are not supported on Calendars, and the two features are mutually exclusive.

In the response, each calendared cost is a JSON array whose length equals number-of-intervals. The meta section MUST include calendar-response-attributes, with calendar-start-time, time-interval-size, number-of-intervals and optionally repeated and cost-type-names. The start time is an HTTP Date value in IMF-fixdate form, which uses GMT, and SHOULD NOT be later than the request date.

For example, a start of Mon, 30 Jun 2019 00:00:00 GMT with 24 intervals of 3600 seconds and repeated of 4 means Monday through Thursday share the same values, so the client only needs a new Calendar for Friday.
sections.eli5: You tick a box saying 'give me the timetable version'. The answer comes back with a list of numbers and a note saying when the list starts and how long each slot lasts.

sections.title: Compatibility with Legacy Clients
sections.content:
A Calendar-aware server MUST implement the base protocol of RFC 7285, and so MUST a Calendar-aware client. Whenever a metric is available as a Calendar array, it MUST also be available as a single value. The single value is the current value of the metric, for clients that want no future values or implement only RFC 7285.

The extension also works with the Multi-Cost extension (RFC 8189), where the calendared array has one entry per requested metric. A server MUST still support constraints on cost types that are not requested as Calendars.
sections.eli5: Old programs that do not know about timetables still get a normal single answer, so nothing breaks for them.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC asks operators to weigh two effects. The first is feedback: like a traffic-aware map service, a Calendar used by many clients can turn a light-traffic choice into congestion, and the RFC cites Braess' Paradox as an example of a less-optimal global outcome. The second is prediction: Calendars tend to reduce the volume of data exchanged compared with many single-cost transactions, and repeated saves more. This holds only when no unexpected events happen.

The RFC recommends timely updates. It is RECOMMENDED that servers providing Calendars also provide the SSE incremental update service of RFC 8895, and clients SHOULD use it. For values that change quickly, a server can avoid sending too many entries by choosing the start time and number of intervals and declaring the Calendar repeated.

The document also notes that it uses the newer JSON specification, RFC 8259, which mandates UTF-8, so implementations using UTF-16 or UTF-32 MUST switch to UTF-8 to interoperate with Calendar-aware peers.
sections.eli5: If everybody picks the same quiet hour because the timetable said so, that hour stops being quiet. So the timetable has to be kept up to date and used with care.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7285 fully apply. Calendars add three concerns: undesirable guidance, confidentiality and availability. On availability, Calendars with future values may help when the server is temporarily unavailable.

On confidentiality, a malicious client could learn about future events and generate massive connections at times when load is expected to be high. The RFC says the server should authenticate clients and use TLS to prevent man-in-the-middle interception, and that clients and servers SHOULD support TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2. These measures do not help against clients with valid credentials that have been subverted into bots for a DDoS attack, so a monitoring system that detects abnormal behavior may still be needed.

On erroneous guidance, Calendar values, especially in repeated Calendars, may be only statistical, and future events may change. If a cost type name appears in more than one Calendar object, the client uses the first one or MAY ignore them all and query the base way.

The document has no IANA actions.
sections.eli5: A schedule of when the network is busy is useful to the bad guys too, so it should only be shared with trusted programs over a private connection.
